svg.aria-label: Figure 2.5: From Cracking Slopes to the King's Chamber — Proportional scale comparison of the Step Pyramid, Bent Pyramid, and Great Pyramid alongside a 3/4 architectural cutaway of the King's Chamber showing five stacked relieving chambers, angled limestone roof slabs, and deflected compression forces
svg.text: Figure 2.5: From Cracking Slopes to the King's Chamber
How a century of pyramid trial and error—and an angled stone roof inside Giza—defeated crushing compression
A. A CENTURY OF TRIAL AND ERROR (TRUE SCALE)
Imhotep stacked 6 cut-limestone tiers to 205 ft (62.5 m)
on a 397 × 358 ft base—Egypt's first monumental stone tomb.
Sneferu built at 54° on soft soil; cracks forced a sharp bend
to 43° at 154 ft (47 m), finishing at 344 ft (105 m) tall.
Lesson learned: steep walls fail without solid rock below.
Great Pyramid of Khufu · Giza, c. 2560 BCE
Anchored on solid limestone bedrock (with an inner rocky hill),
leveled flat within <1 in (2.1 cm): 51.8° slope, 756 ft (230.33 m)
wide base, rising 481 ft (146.6 m) high.
B. INSIDE THE GREAT PYRAMID: BEATING CRUSHING COMPRESSION
Millions of tons of core limestone
lean into an upside-down V, splitting
settling cracks and lifts the tent
lined in Aswan red granite. Standing

g.text: Why a plain flat ceiling fails

svg.text: Panel A pyramids are drawn to exact proportional height, base width, and slope angle along one shared ground baseline.
